explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Jesus says, "…yes, even his own life—he cannot be My disciple." (Luke 14:26) The list starts with the people closest to a person and then lands on the person himself. I think that's the part that makes you sit up straight.

Good guess, but a house never shows up on this list. Jesus names father, mother, wife, children, brothers and sisters, and then adds "…yes, even his own life…" (Luke 14:26). The last item on the list is the person's own life, not a house.

Land makes sense as a guess, since people have held onto their land for ages. But Jesus doesn't name any land here. He lists family and then adds "…yes, even his own life…" (Luke 14:26). The list ends with the person's own life, not property.

Yes, friend. Jesus says, "And whoever does not carry his cross and follow Me cannot be My disciple." (Luke 14:27) Carrying and following go together in that one sentence, so a disciple doesn't get to pick the easier half. I'd pick the easier half every time, and I'm saying it out loud so you don't have to.

A staff is a fair guess for people walking in a crowd on the road. But Jesus doesn't say staff. He says a disciple must carry "…his cross and follow Me…" (Luke 14:27). Nobody leans on this one like a walking stick.

A mat shows up in other Bible stories, like when Jesus tells a man to pick up his mat (Mark 2:11), so I see where that came from. But here Jesus says whoever does not carry "…his cross and follow Me cannot be My disciple." (Luke 14:27) The carrying is tied to the following. I'd say a mat is a lot easier to roll up and tuck under your arm.

That's it, baker. Jesus says the builder will "…first sit down and count the cost to see if he has the resources to complete it?" (Luke 14:28) Sit down first, then count. I wish I had done that before I tried to stamp a hundred cookies with one bowl of dough.

Picking a spot sounds like a smart first move, I'll give you that. But Jesus says the builder first sits down to "…count the cost to see if he has the resources to complete it?" (Luke 14:28) The spot isn't mentioned. The question is whether he can finish.

Hiring workers feels like a logical step, but Jesus never mentions it. He says the builder will "…first sit down and count the cost to see if he has the resources to complete it?" (Luke 14:28) What he first sits down to do is count.

Right, friend. Jesus says, "…everyone who sees it will ridicule him…" (Luke 14:29) Everyone who sees it, not just one or two people. The builder laid the foundation and couldn't finish, and I'd say that's rough on him.

That's a kind thought, and I like it. But Jesus says that "…everyone who sees it will ridicule him…" (Luke 14:29) In His picture, the people who see the unfinished work ridicule the builder. Helping him finish isn't part of it.
If only! Ignoring him would be a mercy, I think. But Jesus says "…everyone who sees it will ridicule him…" (Luke 14:29) What the people who see it do is ridicule him, not ignore him.

Yes, baker. Jesus pictures the king with ten thousand men facing "…the one coming against him with twenty thousand?" (Luke 14:31) That's two soldiers for every one of his. Sitting down to think first sounds pretty smart to me.

Five thousand would be good news for the king with ten thousand. But the number is twenty thousand. Jesus says the other king is "…coming against him with twenty thousand?" (Luke 14:31) That's double, and it's why the first king has to sit down and think.

Seven thousand would have the king with ten thousand feeling pretty good, I bet. But Jesus says the king is facing "…the one coming against him with twenty thousand?" (Luke 14:31) That's twice his army. No wonder he needs to sit down and consider it.

That's right, friend. The king "…will send a delegation while the other king is still far off, to ask for terms of peace." (Luke 14:32) He does it while the other king is still far off, not after the armies are in his face. A smart move, I'd say.

Battle is what he was headed for, so I get it. But Jesus says he sends a delegation "…to ask for terms of peace." (Luke 14:32) The delegation goes out while the other king is still far off. The terms it asks for are peace, not battle.

Trade is a peaceful word, so you were close in spirit. But Jesus says the delegation goes "…to ask for terms of peace." (Luke 14:32) The king isn't looking to do business. He's looking to avoid a fight he can't take on.

True, baker. Jesus says, "In the same way, any one of you who does not give up everything he has cannot be My disciple." (Luke 14:33) He took the builder and the king and tied them straight to the crowd. The words "In the same way…" are the hinge between those two pictures and the people in front of Him.

This one is true, friend. Jesus says, "In the same way, any one of you who does not give up everything he has cannot be My disciple." (Luke 14:33) He brings the builder and the king right back to the crowd. That sentence is the whole point of both pictures.

I can see why that might sound right, but it's the opposite. Jesus says the salt "…is fit neither for the soil nor for the manure pile, and it is thrown out." (Luke 14:35) It's not good for either one. Salt that has lost its savor ends up thrown out.

False is right, friend. Jesus says the salt "…is fit neither for the soil nor for the manure pile, and it is thrown out." (Luke 14:35) It isn't fit for either place, so it gets thrown out. That's a hard fall for something Jesus just called good.
